## Root cause
The limit is the volume's own provisioned IOPS. Since about 18:05 UTC, io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (10 GiB, 1,000 IOPS, /dev/sdf on c6i.xlarge i-1234567890abcdef0_5) has handled a steady stream of 8 KiB writes (no reads) at exactly 1,000 IOPS, which is its provisioned cap. The application sends more writes than the volume will serve, so the extra requests wait in line. Queue length sits at about 1.3 to 1.5 against the alarm threshold of 1.0, and each write takes about 1.5 ms instead of the sub-millisecond time io2 normally gives. Throughput is only about 8 MB/s, so the throughput limit is not the problem. The instance's EBS limits are not the problem either: InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0, and EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at 99%. Fix: raise the volume's provisioned IOPS with an online ModifyVolume. io2 allows up to 500 IOPS per GiB, so this 10 GiB volume can go to 5,000 IOPS without resizing; to go higher, also grow the volume. Size the new value from the application's real write demand, and also consider batching or coalescing the small 8 KiB writes. Before raising it a lot, check the instance's headroom. Other volumes on the same instance are already reading about 131 MB/s. My understanding, not checked here, is that c6i.xlarge's baseline EBS bandwidth is about 1,250 Mbps (about 156 MB/s) and its baseline is about 6,000 IOPS. Going to 5,000 IOPS at 8 KiB adds about 41 MB/s, which would push the instance above that baseline and start using up burst credits. If you need more than that steadily, move to a larger instance size as well.
## Evidence
- The alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength \u003e 1.0) went into ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:04 UTC (1.49 at 18:08–18:10).
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteOps for vol-0123456789abcdef0 has been about 300,000 per 5 minutes in every full period from 18:10 to 19:25 UTC. That is exactly 1,000 IOPS, the provisioned value (describe_volumes: io2, Iops=1000, Size=10 GiB).
- AWS/EBS VolumeReadOps is 0 for the whole window, so all of the load is writes.
- VolumeWriteBytes divided by VolumeWriteOps is about 8,192 bytes per write. Throughput is about 8.2 MB/s, far below the io2 throughput limit, so IOPS is the limit, not throughput.
- VolumeTotalWriteTime is about 448 s per 300,000 writes, or about 1.5 ms per write. VolumeQueueLength averaged about 1.47–1.50 from 18:10 to 19:10 and about 1.27–1.33 after 19:15.
- AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck for i-1234567890abcdef0_5 were 0 in every 5-minute period from 18:05 to 19:30, so the instance's EBS limit was not reached.
- AWS/EC2 EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99% minimum for the whole window, so the instance's burst credits were not running out.
- AWS/EC2 EBSReadBytes on the instance is about 39.3 GB per 5 minutes (about 131 MB/s), coming from the other attached volumes. That leaves limited headroom under the instance's baseline bandwidth if the IOPS raise is large.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 10 GiB, 1000 IOPS)
- i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge)
## Gaps
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no data points for this volume, so the IOPS cap is shown by ops sitting flat at exactly the provisioned value, not by that metric.
- The application's actual write demand (how far it is above 1,000 IOPS) can't be seen at the EBS layer. Check app or OS-level metrics (e.g. iostat await/aqu-sz) to choose the new IOPS value.
- The c6i.xlarge EBS baseline and burst limits come from general knowledge and were not checked with describe_instance_types.
- I did not check whether the application's write pattern or traffic changed at about 18:05 (e.g. a deploy); the instance was launched at 18:05:10, which lines up with when the load started.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "52ac29e4-ff76-497e-970e-8f6455b38585", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "That 18:00 bucket's average gets diluted since it only spans a partial hour within the 6-hour window. I also notice similar activity patterns on Nov 11 and Nov 23 during the 06:00-18:00 window, with comparable peak queue depths around 1.4-1.5.

VolumeThroughputPercentage sits at 100% across the entire window, and combined with VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps at roughly 1000 ops/sec, this strongly confirms the volume is pinned at its provisioned IOPS ceiling. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck shows no data points, which is odd but the flat 1000 IOPS plus 100% throughput is compelling enough evidence on its own.

Without that exceeded-check metric I can't fully separate app-side rate limiting from actual EBS throttling, but the latency signature helps: a queue depth around 1.5 and latency of 1.27–1.5 ms is too elevated for unthrottled io2 Block Express, which should run closer to 0.2–0.5 ms at this load. The latency dip at 19:16 tracking a queue depth drop from 1.49 to 1.27, alongside a brief IOPS dip to 536, fits Little's Law behavior for a throughput-capped server — latency tracking offered concurrency rather than raw demand, which is the classic signature of a capped system rather than pure self-limiting.

I also notice VolumeIdleTime jumping to 60s/min after 19:16 even though the volume was serving 1000 IOPS, which is a metric inconsistency worth flagging as a minor anomaly rather than something material. On the CloudTrail side, I'm second-guessing my jmespath filter on ReadOnly — if that field is a string rather than absent, my filter logic may have excluded real write events, so I want to rerun the lookup for StartInstances and ModifyVolume calls between 17:30 and 18:05:12 to make sure I'm not missing anything, though it's probably not critical to the core finding.

The key question is what's the binding constraint and what needs to change: no ModifyVolume call touched this volume in the window, so its IOPS limit wasn't recently reduced — I want to confirm this with describe_volumes_modifications and one more CloudTrail page. Importantly, EBS-layer write latency has actually been stable or slightly improved since 19:16 (1.27ms) compared to 18:10-19:15 (1.49ms), meaning the elevated latency has been constant since 18:05 when write load increased — so the "last 20 minutes" framing from the user doesn't match what I'm seeing at the EBS layer, and the gap might be explained by OS-level queueing on the guest side rather than the volume itself.

I'm checking whether CWAgent metrics are available for this instance to see guest-side iostat data, then moving to mitigation: the fix is a Limits issue, and I should recommend a ModifyVolume to bump IOPS to around 3,000 — calculated from instance baseline throughput (156.25 MB/s) minus current usage (~139.4 MB/s), leaving roughly 2,060 IOPS of headroom before the instance baseline itself becomes the bottleneck. I also need to flag the 6-hour cooldown between volume modifications so the chosen value is the right one, since there's no second chance soon. Instance IOPS baseline of 6000 isn't a concern here.

This volume has never been modified via ModifyVolume, so it's been sitting at 1000 provisioned IOPS since creation, and there's no CloudWatch agent giving OS-level visibility. Looking at the root cause, the queue length (1.27–1.50) exceeding the 1.0 threshold since 18:08 lines up with the volume being pinned at its provisioned 1000 IOPS cap — VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps confirms 300,000 ops per 5-minute period with throughput percentage at 100%, while actual throughput (7.8 MiB/s) stays well under the binding constraint. I can rule out instance-level EBS limits since checks and balances look healthy, and there's no ModifyVolume event — only the StartInstances call that kicked off this workload. The remaining question is whether real demand exceeds 1000 IOPS or the app is self-throttling, since VolumeIOPSExceededCheck has no data, but the elevated latency (1.3–1.5 ms vs io2's typical sub-millisecond) tracking the queue length points toward genuine throttling.

Concluding that the provisioned IOPS of 1000 is undersized for this workload, I'm recommending a ModifyVolume to raise IOPS to around 3,000, which fits the io2 Block Express ratio and respects the instance's throughput ceiling given the co-tenant gp3 volume's 125 MiB/s draw — noting the 6-hour cooldown between modifications means this needs to be right the first time, with a larger instance type as a fallback if 3,000 IOPS proves insufficient.

An io2 value above about 3,000 IOPS would push the instance above its baseline EBS bandwidth and start using its burst allowance, so the instance would become the next bottleneck. The flat, exact 1,000 IOPS plus about 1.3–1.5 ms latency (well above io2's normal sub-millisecond latency) strongly indicates throttling at the provisioned cap.

Actionable cause to mitigate: raise the provisioned IOPS on vol-0123456789abcdef0 with an online ModifyVolume. ", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "**The binding constraint is the volume itself.** vol-0123456789abcdef0 is provisioned at 1,000 IOPS, and it has been handling exactly 1,000 IOPS of writes since the workload started at about 18:05 UTC. The instance's EBS limits are not what's capping it today. The fix is to raise the volume's provisioned IOPS, but only to about **3,000**, because above that the instance's shared EBS bandwidth becomes the next limit.

**Evidence that the volume is capped**
- The volume is io2, 10 GiB, provisioned at 1,000 IOPS, and has never been modified.
- From 18:10 to 19:30, it handled exactly 300,000 operations every 5 minutes, which is 1,000 per second. CloudWatch reports it at 100% of its provisioned IOPS in every period.
- The load is all writes (zero reads), every one 8 KiB, so only about 7.8 MiB/s. Throughput is nowhere near a limit; the number of operations is.
- Queue length was about 1.49 from 18:08 to 19:15, then about 1.27, against the alarm threshold of 1.0. It crossed at 18:08 and the alarm fired at 18:11:04.
- Write latency was about 1.49 ms, then about 1.27 ms. io2 normally answers in under a millisecond. Operations stay pinned at 1,000 while latency moves with the queue, which is what a capped volume looks like.

**Ruled out**
- **Instance EBS limits:** both of the instance's "limit exceeded" checks stayed at 0 from 18:05 to 19:30, and its EBS burst balances held at 99%. The instance is using about 1,502 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s, against a c6i.xlarge baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (about 149 MiB/s).
- **A configuration change:** the only change to the instance or volume between 17:30 and 19:35 was StartInstances at 18:05:10 by `example-session`. That start is when the write load began. Nothing reduced the volume's capacity.

**What to change**
1. **Raise the IOPS online:** use ModifyVolume to set Iops to about **3,000**. No downtime is needed. As far as I know, io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB (I didn't confirm this in the docs), so 10 GiB is not the limit. Choose the value carefully: EBS only allows one change per volume every 6 hours.
2. **Why stop at about 3,000:** the gp3 volume `vol-1234567890abcdef0_19` (/dev/sdg) on the same instance is using its full 125 MiB/s. That leaves only about 16 MiB/s under the instance's baseline, which is room for roughly 2,000 more 8 KiB writes per second. Going above about 3,000 total would push the instance over its baseline and start using up its burst allowance.
3. **If you need more than about 3,000 steadily:** move to a larger instance size, or reduce how much bandwidth `vol-1234567890abcdef0_19` uses.
4. **On the application side:** batch or combine the 8 KiB writes so each operation carries more data.

**What I couldn't see**
- I can't tell how many writes per second the application actually wants. The volume's IOPS-exceeded metric has no data, and there's no CloudWatch agent or OS-level disk data (such as `iostat`) on the instance. Measure the real demand at the OS before picking the final number.
- At the storage layer, latency did **not** get worse in the last 20 minutes. It has been high since 18:05 and actually dropped slightly after 19:16. Whatever made the application slower more recently is not visible from EBS metrics.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Queue length alarm on io2 volume
**Description:** Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (VolumeQueueLength avg > 1.0 for 3×1 min) entered ALARM at 18:11:04Z on vol-0123456789abcdef0; queue length held ~1.47–1.50 from 18:10 to 19:10, then ~1.27 after 19:15. Avg write latency ~1.49 ms, dropping to ~1.27 ms.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:11:04Z

## Findings

### Cause: Workload saturating io2 provisioned IOPS (1000)
**Description:** io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 (10 GiB, 1000 provisioned IOPS, never modified) has served exactly 1000 IOPS of 8 KiB writes since the workload started at ~18:05Z. It handled 300,000 ops per 5 min at 100% of its provisioned IOPS. Extra requests queue up (queue length ~1.27–1.49 against the 1.0 threshold), and write latency rises to ~1.3–1.5 ms. Throughput (~7.8 MiB/s) is not the limit. The instance's EBS limits and a config change are ruled out.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length-alarm

#### Supporting Observations
- **Volume pinned at provisioned 1000 IOPS:** From 18:10 to 19:30 vol-0123456789abcdef0 sustained exactly ~1000 IOPS (its provisioned io2 IOPS). The workload is 8 KiB writes at ~7.81 MiB/s, and VolumeIdleTime was ~0 from 18:10 to 19:10. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no datapoints.
- **Instance EBS limits not exceeded:** i-1234567890abcdef0_5 (c6i.xlarge): EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at 99%, and InstanceEBSIOPS/ThroughputExceededCheck = 0 throughout. Instance total is ~1500 IOPS and ~133 MiB/s; CPU is ~1%. The other attached volumes are gp3 (3000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s): root vol-1234567890abcdef0_20, vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 and vol-1234567890abcdef0_16.

#### Gaps
- **No OS-level disk metrics (CloudWatch agent):** The CWAgent namespace has no metrics for i-1234567890abcdef0_5. The writing process and the in-guest latency and queue depth can't be seen. The application's real write demand above 1000 IOPS can only be inferred from queue length.
- **Some volume metrics returned no data:** VolumeIOPSExceededCheck, VolumeStalledIOCheck and VolumeAvgWriteLatency for vol-0123456789abcdef0 are listed but returned no datapoints for 18:00–19:33Z. IOPS saturation is therefore shown through consumed ops and throughput percentage, not the exceeded check.

## Other Gaps

### Recent app slowdown not visible in EBS metrics
**Description:** Storage-layer latency has been high since 18:05Z and dropped slightly after 19:16Z; it did not worsen in the last 20 minutes. Whatever slowed the application more recently cannot be seen from EBS metrics.

### Instance reports EbsOptimized=false

The volume is pinned at its 1,000 provisioned IOPS (8 KiB writes, VolumeThroughputPercentage 100%, queue ~1.27–1.51, write latency ~1.3–1.5 ms). The instance has ~16 MiB/s of EBS headroom (132.9 of ~149 MiB/s, mostly gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 at 125 MiB/s), enough for about 2,000 more 8 KiB IOPS. At 3,000 IOPS total instance traffic is ~148 MiB/s, just under baseline. EBS allows one modification every 6 hours, so the value must be right first time.
